title: Hostile Marriages Heal Slower
text:
At Ohio State University, the psychologist Janice Kiecolt-Glaser and her husband, the immunologist Ronald Glaser, spent years studying how stress affects the body. In one study they invited 42 married couples to stay overnight in a hospital research unit on two separate occasions.

On each visit, a small suction device raised tiny blisters on each person's forearm, creating standardized wounds that the researchers could watch heal. On the first visit, the couples then had a supportive conversation, discussing something they each wanted to change about themselves while the partner offered help. On the second visit they discussed a topic of ongoing disagreement in their marriage. The researchers recorded the conversations, coded how hostile each couple was, and took blood samples.

The wounds healed more slowly after the conflict discussion than after the supportive one. The differences between couples were even more striking. Couples who were highly hostile during both visits, with sarcasm, criticism and put-downs, healed at only about 60 percent of the speed of couples low in hostility. They also showed higher levels of inflammatory substances in the blood after their conflicts.

The study offered a concrete physical picture of how a hostile marriage can wear on health over years.
lesson: How you argue at home affects your body, not just your mood. Criticism and contempt carry a physical cost for both partners.
people: Janice Kiecolt-Glaser, Timothy Loving, Ronald Glaser and colleagues
source: Kiecolt-Glaser, J. K., Loving, T. J., Stowell, J. R., Malarkey, W. B., Lemeshow, S., Dickinson, S. L., and Glaser, R. (2005). Hostile marital interactions, proinflammatory cytokines, and wound healing. Archives of General Psychiatry, 62(12), 1377-1384.
